concept.name: Constant-product market maker
concept.definition: A constant-product market maker (CPMM) is the canonical AMM pricing rule in which the product of a pool's two token reserves must remain constant across trades (x·y=k), so the marginal price is the ratio of reserves and each trade moves the price along a hyperbola.
concept.intuition: The pool is a balanced scale: remove some of one token and the other must grow so their product never shrinks — which is why big orders get progressively worse prices.
concept.mechanics: A swap of Δx of token X for token Y must satisfy (x+Δx)(y−Δy)=k (before fees), giving output Δy = y·Δx/(x+Δx). The instantaneous price is y/x, so price impact grows quadratically with trade size relative to depth; a fee (e.g. 0.3% in Uniswap v2) is taken from the input and accrues to LPs, making k grow slightly per trade.
concept.formula: x · y = k, where x, y are token reserves and k is the invariant; output for input Δx: Δy = y·Δx / (x + Δx) (ignoring fees).
concept.failure_modes: The full-range design spreads liquidity from 0 to ∞, so most capital sits unused and large trades suffer severe price impact in thin pools; when one token trends, arbitrage continuously extracts value from LPs (impermanent loss).
concept.misconceptions: The invariant does not keep k exactly constant — fees make k grow, and k changes whenever liquidity is added or removed. x·y=k also does not prevent LPs from losing money to price divergence.
concept.example: A pool holds 10 ETH and 40,000 USDC (k=400,000, price 4,000 USDC/ETH). Buying 1 ETH requires paying 40,000×1/9 ≈ 4,444 USDC — about 11% above the quoted price, illustrating price impact at 10% of pool depth.
